For the first years after Pentecost the apostles preached in Jerusalem, confirming the covenant with many in Israel. Then Stephen was stoned, persecution scattered the church, Philip preached in Samaria, Paul was called as apostle to the Gentiles, and Peter went to Cornelius. The week of the covenant's confirmation to Israel came to its end, and the door opened to the nations.
Acts 8:1-5: scattered through Judea and Samaria.
Acts 9:15: a chosen instrument to carry my name before the Gentiles.
Acts 13:46: since you thrust it aside, we turn to the Gentiles.
Some preterists place the last week at AD 66-73 instead, with its middle at the destruction of the temple in AD 70.
What are the main ways of reading the seventy weeks?
Four: the continuous messianic count (partial preterist and many Reformed), the dispensational gap, the critical Maccabean view, and the symbolic view.

The messianic view counts the weeks straight through to Christ. The dispensational view stops the clock after the 69th week and places the 70th in a future tribulation. The critical view reads the whole prophecy as written in the 160s BC about Antiochus IV. The symbolic view treats the weeks as an era stretching from Cyrus to the second coming. The 70-square chart on this page lets you see each one.
Messianic: E. J. Young, many Reformed and partial preterist writers.
Gap: Robert Anderson, Harold Hoehner, most dispensationalists.
Critical: most modern academic commentaries.
Each view has a best case; they are set out side by side on this page.
Where did the gap view come from?
Some early writers placed part of the last week near the end, but a systematic gap with a future Antichrist treaty developed with 19th-century futurism and dispensationalism.

Irenaeus and Hippolytus linked the Antichrist to half a week at the end, so the idea of a future half-week is old. But many early writers, including Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, Eusebius and Augustine, related the weeks to Christ's first coming. The detailed gap model, with a seven-year treaty and a pre-tribulation rapture, took shape in the work of Darby, Robert Anderson's The Coming Prince (1881) and the Scofield Bible.
Hippolytus, Commentary on Daniel: the last week at the end, split by the Antichrist.
Tertullian, Against the Jews 8: the weeks reach Christ and the destruction of Jerusalem.
Robert Anderson, The Coming Prince (1881): the 360-day count to AD 32.
Dispensationalists point to Irenaeus and Hippolytus as early witnesses to a future final week.
Why do many scholars think Daniel 9 is about Antiochus IV?
Because Daniel 8 and 11 clearly describe Antiochus, and they date the book to his time. But Daniel 9's numbers and events fit Christ better.

Daniel 8 names Greece and describes a king who desecrates the temple and stops the sacrifice, which Antiochus did in 167 BC. Critical scholars read chapter 9 the same way, with the anointed one as Onias III. But Antiochus did not destroy the city and sanctuary (9:26), the count falls well short of 490 years, and Jesus treated the abomination of desolation as future in his own day.
1 Maccabees 1:54: the abomination set up on the altar in 167 BC.
Matthew 24:15: Jesus refers to Daniel's abomination as still to come.
Critical scholars respond that apocalyptic numbers are schematic, and that Jesus reapplied Daniel's language to new events.
How did Jesus use Daniel?
He called himself the Son of Man of Daniel 7, announced that the time was fulfilled, and warned that Daniel's abomination of desolation would come on that generation.

Jesus' favourite title came from Daniel 7:13. At his trial he said the high priest would see the Son of Man seated at the right hand and coming with the clouds (Matthew 26:64). He told the disciples to flee Judea when they saw the abomination Daniel spoke of. Each use ties Daniel to his own ministry and that generation.
Mark 1:15: the time is fulfilled.
Matthew 26:64: you will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds.
Matthew 24:15-16: let those in Judea flee.
Futurists agree Jesus is the Son of Man, but read his coming on the clouds as the second coming.
Is the Son of Man's coming in Daniel 7 the second coming?
In Daniel 7 the Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days, upward, to receive a kingdom. That is the ascension.

Daniel sees one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days, and given dominion, glory and a kingdom. The movement is toward God, not toward earth. Jesus ascended in a cloud and sat at God's right hand, receiving all authority (Matthew 28:18). His “coming on the clouds” in judgement on Jerusalem showed that enthronement.
Acts 1:9: a cloud took him out of their sight.
Matthew 28:18: all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.
Ephesians 1:20-22: seated at his right hand, far above all rule.
Futurists read Daniel 7:13 with Revelation 1:7 as the visible second coming.
What is still future on a partial preterist reading?
Christ's bodily return, the resurrection of the dead, the final judgement, and the full renewal of creation.

Partial preterism is not the view that everything has happened. Acts 1:11 promises Jesus will come back in the same way he went. 1 Thessalonians 4 and 1 Corinthians 15 describe the resurrection at his coming. Revelation 20:11-15 describes the final judgement. These remain the Christian hope. The passage map on this page marks each text as fulfilled, future, or both.
Acts 1:11: this same Jesus will come in the same way.
1 Corinthians 15:23-26: the last enemy to be destroyed is death.
Revelation 20:12: the dead were judged by what they had done.
Full preterists say even these were fulfilled in AD 70; partial preterists and every historic creed reject that.
How do Daniel's visions fit together?

Daniel 2 and 7 give the four kingdoms ending with Rome and God's kingdom; Daniel 8 and 11 zoom in on Greece and Antiochus; Daniel 9 sets the clock to the Messiah; Daniel 12 ends with the shattering of the holy people's power.

Daniel 2 and 7 run in parallel: Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome, and then the kingdom of God set up in Rome's days. Daniel 8 and 11 give detail on the Greek period and Antiochus' persecution. Daniel 9 gives the time to the Messiah and the destruction that follows his rejection. Daniel 12 says all these things would be finished when the power of the holy people was shattered: the end of the old covenant order in AD 70.
Daniel 2:44: in the days of those kings.
Daniel 12:7: when the shattering of the power of the holy people comes to an end, all these things will be finished.
Futurists see a revived Rome and the Antichrist at the end of several of these visions.
What principles help us read time prophecies well?
Read the time words plainly, let the New Testament interpret the Old, look first for a fulfilment the Bible itself names, and do not read the news into the text.

First, take time statements as their first hearers would: “near” means near. Second, follow the apostles' own interpretations of the prophets. Third, look for the fulfilment the Bible names before adding a second one. Fourth, read symbols as the prophets used them: falling stars are the fall of rulers (Isaiah 13:10). Fifth, keep the great certainties: Christ's return, resurrection and judgement.
Isaiah 13:10, 19: stars darkened at the fall of Babylon.
Acts 2:16: this is what was spoken.
Revelation 22:10: do not seal up the words, for the time is near.
Futurists add that some prophecies have near and far fulfilments, so the first-century fulfilment may not be the last.
Why does the seventy weeks prophecy matter?
Because it shows God fixed the time of the Messiah five centuries in advance, and because it decides whether we expect a future seven-year tribulation.

A prophecy that names the time of the Messiah's coming and death, and the destruction of the temple that followed, is a powerful witness to Jesus. It also governs much of modern prophecy teaching: the seven-year tribulation, the Antichrist's treaty and the rebuilt temple all depend on placing the 70th week in the future. Reading it as fulfilled keeps Christ at the centre of the prophecy.
Luke 24:27: beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.
Galatians 4:4: when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son.
Dispensationalists see the prophecy as equally Christ-centred, with the 70th week showing his final victory over the Antichrist.

The messianic count
The weeks run from the decree to the Messiah, who is cut off in the middle of the last week and confirms the new covenant; the city falls in AD 70. This is the reading this study follows.
The dispensational gap
The clock stops after the 69th week; the 70th is a future seven-year tribulation with an Antichrist treaty and a rebuilt temple.
The symbolic reading
The weeks are symbolic eras from Cyrus to the end, with the last week the church age.
The critical reading
Daniel 9 describes the Maccabean crisis, with Antiochus IV as the desolator, written about 165 BC.
